Really addicting, at first I went ah it's simple just mash punch or ki buttons. Oh wait a minute I forgot we got the dashes, the warps, the counters, the warp counters, ok well let's go through Goku's campaign and learn. Got clapped by Oozaru Vegeta for HOURS. Stayed up late grinding. Finally conceded and went back to training mode. Still struggled but finally got it. Now, it's a strange design choice to put a ridiculously tough fight, at least for people new to the game/series, as one of the first fights of Goku's story mode, but hey it toughened me up for the long haul. 

Long story short. Advice for playing the story or potentially against AI:

- Play the training for a while, especially if you are new to the series, DOUBLE ESPECIALLY if you are new to the series AND fighting games. If you don't know how to warp counter, dragon dash, and know most of the basic/intermediate maneuvers from the tutorials, you will get pummeled. Definitely learn how to dodge most general special blasts as well (dash sideways if far away, can follow up with a Dragon Dash, can tap block right before it hits you as well but that is way tougher.).

- Maybe don't do Goku's story first or don't be afraid to switch it up or go back to training when you are getting your face beat in. I am a stubborn SOB and should have went back to training an hour earlier than I did.

- Get your defense right. I focused on attacking and cool combos first and my defense was garbage, didn't matter that I was getting some good combos off when I'm getting hit by most attacks. 

- Abuse specials, ki blasts, and full ki charging into Sparking mode if you need to. AI usually blocks special ki blasts instead of dodging, at least as I have seen so far. This allows you to stack up some chip damage. Sparking mode lets you mash X and potentially get an easy 20 punch combo. 

Loving the game. I miss the old days of playing a game, getting in-game currency, and unlocking more characters, costumes, items, etc. It's a fantastic gameplay loop and one I am so happy this game went with that old school approach. If you are a Dragonball fan it's a no brainer if the price works for you. If you aren't a Dragonball fan see if you like the combat style, it is tough at first but once you are trading blows and flying around it looks like you are playing a cutscene. 

Fun to see alternate routes in the story as well, another bonus for Dragonball fans. Can't wait to keep playing.

Lastly, rest in peace Toriyama sensei, your work has had a profound impact on my life and you are missed, we will treasure this series for hundreds of years to come <3

I’ve been waiting this game for years, probably over a decade. 
My favorite Dragon Ball game is Budokai Tenkaichi 3 and I played it a lot. This new game feels like BT3 with Super characters, some minor gameplay changes and unfortunately a few missing characters that really should’ve been added as DLC by now.
The story mode was fine, it included some what if scenarios that I really enjoyed. Honestly, I wish the game focused entirely on this direction, because replaying the same story over and over in every game is boring, at least for me. Still, it’s better than nothing.
Custom Battle is amazing. I knew right away I’d spend a lot of hours into it, recreating the what ifs I used to watch on YouTube, imagining in my head or discussing with friends. It could definitely be improved, but even as it is, it gives the game infinite replay value for me.

Now for the negatives.
Online was ridiculously unbalanced at launch and the developers took way too long to fix it, which drove away 90% of the player base. The game desperately needs more gamemodes (like Survival, Mission 100 or additional what if stories) as well as new outfits and accessories for all characters. The customization potential would be incredible: imagine Goku in old Saiyan armor or Frieza dressed as Goku with a saiyan tail. Some characters don’t even have a second outfit, which is unacceptable considering even BT3 gave everyone at least one alternate color.
The DLC situation is also very bad. The release time is way too slow. By now, we should’ve had most GT characters, full Daima, and maybe even some unique what if fighters like Gohan Black or Gohkan.

Do I recommend this game?
Yes but only on sale. It’s still a great Dragon Ball experience and it has the potential to become probably the best. 
But unless the developers do something, mods are the only way to experience the game’s true potential.

As someone who has played a ton of Dragon Ball games, bought plenty of season passes, and genuinely loves this franchise, the way DRAGON BALL: Sparking! ZERO is being monetized feels increasingly predatory.

The base game costs $69.99. The Deluxe Edition costs $99.99. The Ultimate Edition costs $109.99. The Season Pass costs $34.99 separately.

I bought the Deluxe Edition because it included the Season Pass. Paying nearly $100 upfront reasonably suggested that I was buying the game together with its meaningful post-launch content—not temporary access to the first few packs before being charged again for the expansion that actually resembles a major expansion.

Instead, the Season Pass was filled out with content including Shallot, the protagonist of a mobile game, while Super Limit-Breaking NEO is being separated from it and sold as another DLC. This is not a minor costume pack. Bandai Namco advertises 33 playable characters, a new solo mode, four Episode Battles, additional Extra Battles, and four stages.

Even “33 characters” needs context but transformations are counted as separate roster entries: Vegeta (GT) and Super Saiyan Vegeta (GT) count separately, as do Trunks (GT) and Super Saiyan Trunks (GT), while Super Saiyan Bardock is another entry rather than a transformation for the Bardock already in the game. So this is not 33 distinct characters.

Many of the actual characters are not new to Budokai Tenkaichi either. Grandpa Gohan, Mercenary Tao, Demon King Piccolo, Zangya, Pikkon, Super 17, Nam, Android 8, General Blue, Fasha, Salza, Supreme Kai, Uub, King Vegeta, and Nuova Shenron were already playable in Budokai Tenkaichi 3.

Yes, recreating them for a modern engine required models, animations, effects, balancing, voice work, and development time. The problem is the product structure: established characters from the previous major game were omitted from the $70 successor, excluded from the $35 Season Pass, and reserved for another paid expansion after Deluxe and Ultimate Edition customers had already paid $100–$110.

I understand the technical defense that the Season Pass listed four specific packs and did not promise every DLC forever. But that does not erase the expectation created by selling premium editions around something literally called a Season Pass especially when the largest post-launch expansion is excluded.

The pass was not communicated cleanly either. On June 23, 2025, the official Steam description was changed to say it included “34 DLC Packs.” On September 24, it was changed to “4 DLC Packs.” It was probably a typo, but the official sales page displayed it for roughly three months. Customers should not have to reverse-engineer what the publisher intended its own product description to say.

I remember when a new game cost $60 and generally felt complete. Now the entry price is $70, premium editions cost $100–$110, and major content is still carved out and sold separately.

Bandai Namco reported 5.4 million copies sold by the end of March 2025. At the full $69.99 list price, that represents roughly $377.9 million in gross retail value. That is not the company’s actual revenue or profit: copies were sold across several platforms, at different prices, and taxes, refunds, development, marketing, licensing, distribution, and storefront fees all matter.

But the scale is still enormous. Steam takes 30% of the first $10 million, 25% between $10 million and $50 million, and 20% above $50 million. In a purely illustrative all-Steam, full-price scenario, Steam would receive about $78.6 million and roughly $299.4 million would remain on the publisher side before other expenses.

Now suppose this DLC costs $29.99. At only 10% adoption among 5.4 million owners, that is $16.2 million gross and about $12.96 million remaining after a 20% Steam share. At 25%, it is $40.5 million gross and about $32.4 million remaining. At 50%, it is $81 million gross and about $64.8 million remaining.

Again, those are illustrations, not profit estimates. The point is that even a modest purchase rate generates millions more from customers who may already have paid $100 or $110.

At $29.99, a Deluxe Edition buyer would be at about $129.98 and an Ultimate Edition buyer at about $139.98, before the two $14.99 anime music packs and other extras.

I am not arguing that developers should work for free or that every expansion must be included forever. I am arguing that customers who paid extra specifically for a Season Pass should not feel they bought the wrong premium edition when the largest expansion arrives.

At minimum, Season Pass, Deluxe Edition, and Ultimate Edition owners should receive Super Limit-Breaking NEO at a substantial discount or a reasonably priced upgrade path. Ideally, it should be included for those customers as recognition that they already paid a premium for the game and its post-launch content.

Dividing one game into a $70 base product, $100–$110 premium editions, a separate Season Pass, music packs, small character packs, and then another major expansion is not rewarding loyal fans. It is testing how many times those fans can be charged for the same game before they finally stop paying.

[h1]"The power comes in response to a need, Not a desire."[/h1]

[h1]Introduction[/h1]
From the first moment I watched Dragonball Z as a child, I was enamoured by the characters and world. And by a story of how being different doesn't exclude you, how passion can push you to greater heights and how being beaten only makes you stronger. These have echoed within me, and ever since, Dragonball and all of its iterations have held a foundation within my life, so when I heard there was a new Budokai Tenkaichi game coming out, suffice to say I was overwhelmingly excited to get my hands on it. But did it live up to the hype, or was it fated to never see a power level over 9000?

[table]
[tr]
 [th][b]🟩 Positives[/b][/th]
 [th][b]🟥 Negatives[/b][/th]
[/tr]
[tr]
 [td]🟩 An enormous repertoire of 180+ fighters that range across multiple eras, series' and iterations.

🟩 The original storylines from the series, with special "What if" challenges for those daring enough to attempt them.

🟩 Frenetic and skill-based combat that will test your abilities and understanding of mechanics from the very moment you start.

🟩 A genuinely impressive visual take on the anime style that only helps diversify the world and uniquely identify your favourite characters.[/td]
 [td]🟥 Some of the campaign characters aren't delivered an equal portion of the storyline even if they are canonically a part of more, which is a little disappointing.

🟥 Dialogue during the campaign takes a while to transition to the next scene, you can skip it but sometimes the sequences are about to transition mid-skip and you end up skipping the new scene.[/td]
[/tr]
[/table]

[h1]Story[/h1]
I don't think I have to spend too long here, as the game essentially delivers the standard Dragonball Z storyline and onwards for 7 characters.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3346751528

The "What If" challenges do offer arcs to the plot but don't significantly alter the plot and are more often just there to add difficulty to the campaign.

The dialogue is well-written, and the campaign proceeds at a reasonable pace.

[h1]Gameplay Analysis[/h1]
[h3]Break through...THE LIMIT![/h3]
The bread and butter of Dragonball Sparking! Zero is combat, but you might be surprised by how deep it is. There's a decent skill gap to cross to hold your ground in any major conflict, and the range of techniques and skills you can utilise can be a little overwhelming when starting.

It's more complex than simply spamming attacks or throwing your opponent and hitting them with big energy blasts. You will need to be able to manoeuvre the rather sizable battlefields using movement skills such as steps and dashes, and further improving your understanding of how they work to cross even greater distances more easily.

The actual fighting mechanics are also largely more complex than the standard Dragonball game, by employing guards, counters, and properly chaining combos and ki blasts will greatly determine your success rate.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3346754698

On top of the abundance of techniques above, you will also have to gain some mastery over skills your characters can use, such as larger-scale energy blasts and character-specific techniques that can help turn the tide of battle.

Accessories largely change combat functionality by adding extra layers to the already considerable repertoire where combining these can turn battles in your favour, but understanding what they do and how they blend is tricky, to say the least.

I recommend heading to the "Battle Training" section before you get into the game to get some good foundational experience before you set up bad habits.

[h3]I am the hope of the universe. I am the answer to all living things that cry out for peace.[/h3]
There is an enormous catalogue of characters in this game, and a majority of them feel unique (quite a lot are Goku iterations, so not all). Not all are available to play with from the start, so you will have to spend some time grinding out in-game currencies to unlock them, which can be time-consuming, but it makes them feel worthwhile.

Each character has its nuances and can take some time to learn, not only to play but also to fight against. Have some patience, play around with combos and learn the mechanics at your own pace.

[h1]Audio and Visual[/h1]
The art and visual style of Sparking! Zero is astounding, delivering a crisp and stunning take on the anime aesthetic. The world is astoundingly well-detailed, and combined with the destructive effects you can cause upon it, the immersion level is high. Every character has been lovingly integrated into this game to be astoundingly unique, from how they stand and move to how they fight and throw ki-blasts.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3346752749

The audio style is of similarly high quality, a lot of the original voice actors have returned to voice for the game, (I played with English dub as it's what I'm used to) and each animation comes with a vibrant array of audio effects to make your attacks all feel truly impactful.

[h1]Performance and Specifications[/h1]
I had no issues running this game on Ultra settings at 2560 x 1440 resolution, and I also didn't notice any graphical or performance bugs during my current play time.
RAM: Kingston Fury Beast 64GB 6000MHZ DDR5
CPU: Intel Core i9 14900K 24 Core
GPU: MSI Gaming X GeForce RTX 4090 24GB

[h1]Final Thoughts - Flawless[/h1]
[url=https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2529084785]Review chart here.[/url]
While there are some areas I would have improved upon if I were involved in the development to further improve some quality of life aspects and the story-telling experience, I still believe this is hands down the best Dragonball game I have ever played, by far surpassing even the legendary Budokai Tenkaichi 3, and probably even takes the crown for best fighting game I've ever played. The animations, story-telling, art style, skill gap for combat and just about every aspect of this game are astounding, and I am genuinely excited to play even more of this incredible title. I understand that there may be a caveat here that you need to be a Dragonball fan to enjoy it quite as much as I did, but I also think this is probably a great entry point for non-fans to get into the series.

[h1]Dragon Ball Sparking Zero, A Timeless Classic, Reimagined[/h1]
Dragon Ball Sparking Zero is the latest game in the Budokai Tenkaichi series, where Dragon Ball characters form teams to fight in 3D arenas that focus more on fun and realistic aspects of the Dragon Ball universe rather than a balanced fighter experience. 

The game might look simplistic at first glance, with gameplay mechanics that make it a button smasher at times, but beneath a deceptive flow of gameplay (and horrendous tutorials) Sparking Zero hides a title that requires a lot of finesse to make the most out of combos and special attacks. Bandai Namco and Spike Chunsoft bring a legendary successor to the Budokai Tenkaichi games.

[h1] What Makes It Worth Playing? [/h1]
Sparking Zero enhances the gameplay of the classic formula by expanding the roster with new characters, making techniques tracking better at following opponents, and having a big visual upgrade from the classic games. The game is eye candy, with fluid detailed animations, destruction of environments, light effects, and models that make the player believe they are in an episode of Dragon Ball.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3354016860

Another reason to get the game is that not only does it boast iconic battles such as Goky SSJ VS Frieza in Namek, but it also creates new ones through the "What If" scenarios. These divergent paths go all the way from Goku defeating Cell or Majin Boo earlier to instead of getting Goku Black, we get Gohan Black, making for entertaining scenarios that let the developers play with new ideas and exciting content that adds value to the story mode. 

[H1] This is how Sparking Zero Works[/h1]
The game features fast-paced battles where decisions we take every second can dictate a win or a defeat, and the game uses a bit of button smashing in the melee combos but finesses in the techniques as smashing a vanishing attack or Kamehameha results in nothing. To articulate this better, if Kamehameha is a skill that needs RB+B, you have to press both buttons, once, without spamming at the same time to get the skill to activate.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3354017708

Some menus such as transformations and active power-ups have been simplified to reach a modern audience that didn't grow up with the classic Budokai games, and Sparking Zero at its core is a defensive game where knowing how to vanish and block helps greatly when it comes to obliterating foes. The game uses Ki in multiple bars, which require smart use in battle to get the most out of it and knowing where to charge up as it leaves one wide open. The result is a game that is easy to pick up but hard to master, especially when we consider the huge roster of characters that are all unique and feature different stats, skills, and gameplay styles.

[h1] The DP system, a Blessing and a Curse [/h1]
Sparking Zero uses a system called DP (Destruction Points) to evaluate how powerful characters are in the lore and gameplay. The game limits you to 15 DP total for team battles, with powerful characters such as Gogeta or Vegito costing 10 each while basic fighters like Goku Black or Vegeta cost 5. The idea here is to make a balanced team that can tackle multiple strategies and adapt to enemies on the fly, which is challenging and exciting as there is not enough DP to create a dream team.

However, that is not to say amazing teams cannot be made. While at a simple glance, one might think "I put Ultra Instinct Goku and Vegeta" there are characters that can thwart a simplistic approach. Captain Ginyu can swap bodies and ruin everything, Yajirobe can replenish HP and waste away good fighters little by little and even Master Roshi can deal devastating damage. 

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3354017176

It is in this philosophy that teams can have multiple powerful fighters, like Gogeta and Broly of Super while using Mr Satan and Roshi to block body change or avoid the former two from being exhausted due to weaker opponents.  That is without even mentioning transformations, fusions, and much more, which can make a 15 DP team reach 22 as the battle progresses. Sadly, the DP system also means making teams such as Goku Ultra Instinct and Berrus impossible to combine. However, it is still a system that I appreciate in terms of design philosophy. 

[h1] Price Point Analysis and Replayability[/h1]

For 70 bucks, I can easily recommend this to Dragon Ball fans who will get to enjoy new stories and the multiplayer mode with the huge roster. However, for non-Dragon Ball fans, it becomes a tricky recommendation. The game is unbalanced, making some characters busted and a pain to deal with in ranked, while at the same time, the story mode can be short overall at 8-10 hours, which leaves only multiplayer as the only content available. Adding to the gripes that the game explains mechanics poorly can result in a bad experience that leaves more to be desired. 

Thus, if you are unsure, I would wait for a sale of the game for those who are no big fans of Dragon Ball. For replayability, as long as multiplayer is enjoyable to you, the game is infinite and has a good value to it.

[h1] Conclusion [/h1]

Sparking Zero is the dream of every Dragon Ball fan: huge roster, impressive graphics, and a game that not only retells the story of Goku but adds more to it. The game is incredibly colorful, with a vibrant palette it that reinforces how spectacular and intense the battles are. One of the best Dragon Ball games out there to ever be made, being in direct competition with a select few such as Kakarot, Sparking Zero manages to reimagine and revitalize the core formula of Budokai Tenkaichi to new heights.

TL;DR - Worth it for fans of arena fighters and Dragon Ball. Gameplay feels good and it features many (but not all) fan favorite characters. Worth it on a decent discount. 

Now, here's the thing - I've been a fan of Budokai games since the PS2 era, and they give some nice memories. 

Sparking Zero is a modernized Tenkaichi (Sparking) game, with updated graphics and combat mechanics. 

The combat feels fluid, with a few game patches it has gotten a lot more balanced so it can be good fun for competitive players. 

It can also be played P1vP2 locally, so the level of fun pretty much depends on you. 

The soundtrack is decent but the anime tracks that you have to purchase individually if you don't buy the Deluxe+ are extremely overpriced.

Now the mixed : Online play is connection and FPS dependent, so if your opponent has 40 FPS and you 60 your game will feel like a slow-motion movie. The story mode is quite basic and some characters don't even have complete sagas for them (e.g. Vegeta doesn't even explore most of the Super anime), and there aren't that many cutscenes - you might get some title cards and some overlaid text - the Narrator is also not there most of the time.

You can create Custom Battles as well, but it takes a lot of effort and it might be for you, it wasn't really for me.

So the single player modes are kinda lacking, and the main focus is on multiplayer/online play.

And the main problem of the game is exactly there: the competitive community. People will try to do anything for a win of imaginary worthless online points : exploit the game, lag-switch, disconnect so that they don't lose points.. Unless you can handle such levels of toxicity and "stress", I recommend playing with friends/family for fun. Every online game mode of the game (even Player/Unranked match) is extremely toxic 90% of the time.

So why do I recommend it?

At the end of the day it's Dragon Ball - a great nostalgic feeling comes when I start it up, it looks good, runs good and even against the CPU it can be a fun challenge. On PC you also get the option to add mods to further increase your enjoyment.

It could've been great, ended up being good. Good enough, I guess.

As someone who put countless hours into BT2 and BT3 back in the day, I feel obligated to leave a review.

This game is an amazing sequel to the series and continues the trend of being a true DB simulator, bringing back 90% of the roster while introducing DBS and Daima characters. It’s not the most technical or competitive DB fighting game but that was never what the series was about. Instead we get a gorgeous arena fighter with a large selection of characters, with obviously huge amounts of love poured into the game and so many small details that Spike Chunsoft added as reference to the anime.


The positives:
- Huge roster: With 182 characters/transformations to choose from, everyone should be able to find a favorite character to re-enact fights or create their own
- Beautiful graphics and destructible stages: These really help sell the DB simulator and the series has never look better
- Interesting story mode: With so many DB/Z/GT/S games just rehashing the same story, the devs did a good job packaging it up to keep it fresh. The new what-ifs add some nice twists too 
- Fast paced combat: While not as technical as DBFZ, this game still offers really fast paced and fun combos that both new players and BT veterans can pick up to master
- The new custom battle mode allows you to create your own mini-episodes!

The Neutral:
-Character customization is awesome but also lacking: The ability to kit your favorite characters out with capsules is back but the amount of initial capsules is a bit lacking. Perhaps this will change as I get to a higher player level. Also, not being able to put halos or scouters on all characters is disappointing to see
- Outfit selection is great for the main trio but poor for everyone else: Goku, Vegeta, and Gohan have a decent selection of outfits but everyone else either doesn’t have any or are limited to small variations. This sticks out even more with the BT2/3 alt colors seemingly absent from the game
- Shenron wishes are underwhelming: in the past games, we had 8+ characters available from wishing, compared to only two this time around. Minor issue but still odd to see 

The negatives:
- Lack of stages: While the stage destruction and detail is amazing, having only 12 stages feels really limiting. Especially with major ones that were part of the original games not making the cut like Kami’s Tower, Mountain Road, or Kame’s House. Hopefully we will get more stages added along alongside DLC and free updates 
- Strange roster omissions: Having majority of the OGDB characters get cut is a little lame but can be remedied with DLC but things like Shin, Goku (Teen)/Kid Gohan’s Oozaru form, Base Garlic Jr,, GT Vegeta Base & SSJ, or even alternate costumes for Broly (Z) and Frieza Soldier seems odd. Hopefully fleshed out with future updates

If you love DB and/or played the original BT games back on PS2/GC, I highly suggest you get this game. Well worth the money and I am sure this game will get plenty of support going forward, adding the various missing stages and characters (fingers crossed for manga characters and OVA characters) to continue creating our ultimate DB fantasies.

This game so far gets a solid 9/10 from me at its current launch state.

You like Dragon ball? Thinking about picking up this game just to have a recent DB game to play? Don't do it. 

TL;DR
Sparking Zero legit launched with a "half done" story mode and basic battle modes like duel and world tournament for a full $65 USD giving a "bare bones" game. So much so, basic features from earlier entries  in the same franchise (from 20 year old games on inferior tech) put Sparking Zero to shame. A January 2026 update added Mission 100 mode and there are still problems even a year after launch (such as a known bug in Mission 78 that causes the player to lose immediately after the character intros). Even as a DBZ fanboy I cannot in good conscience recommend Sparking Zero.      

1.) Story Mode
If you are considering about picking up Sparking Zero to "experience" the story of DBZ then I have some bad news for you as Sparking Zero's story mode is very much underwhelming. Sparking Zero's "episode battle" is an extremely abridged. This is NOT start at the Saiyan saga and proceed your way through the story fighting as various characters like in the PS2/3 games. No, instead the Story focus on 8 characters (Goku, Vegeta, Gohan, Piccolo, Trunks, Frieza, Goku Black and Jiren) Also the story mode will skip ENTIRE SAGAS of a character's story. For example, Gohan's story mode skips the saiyan saga, namek/frieza saga and android saga to begin Gohan's FIRST story battle in the hyperbolic time chamber/room of spirit & time in the CELL SAGA. Previous installments on the PS2 did a significantly better job telling the story of DBZ on inferior hardware with tech limitations so there is no excuse for the story mode in a DBZ game known for faithfully retelling the story of DBZ/Movies to skip so much of DBZ's history (which would have been "content" which Sparking Zero sorely lacks imo)  Literally all Sparking Zero had to do to "clear" was copy & paste from DBZ:BT2/3. Go through the major sagas (Saiyan Saga, Frieza Saga , Cell Saga, Buu Saga) then go through the new sagas in DBZ Super. That's it. That's how low the bar was that Sparking Zero could NOT clear.

Only praise I can offer Sparking Zero is the what if scenarios. Basically in certain fights if certain conditions are met aka "defeat the opponent in a specific time limit (which is not explained well at all, roughly 60-90 seconds) there will be a short branching "what if" path. For example, what if Goku went Super Saiyan vs Vegeta in the Saiyan saga. 

2.) Premium Price for Barebones Content
So if the Sparking Zero's story mode is lackluster then what else is there to do in the game? Exactly. Story mode is the bulk of a DBZ game's content. What you have left is: 

A.) Battle mode for single battles or team battles- Fight CPUs offline or players online.
B.) World Tournament Mode - Compete in Tournaments offline or online.
C.) Custom Battle - Play custom scenarios made by the developers, players or make your own. 
D.) Mission 100 - Free DLC as of January 2026

Sparking Zero custom battle mode is clearly where the developers intended players to spend time making and sharing their creations. In theory, it works. Have the Sparking Zero community's imagination to supply an endless amount of content. On principle, however, it's a slap to the face.  Imagine if you order a pizza from Pizza Hut expecting to get a box with a cooked pizza inside only to receive a few cooked slices along with uncooked ingredients Pizza Hut wants you to assembly and cook yourself to make your own custom pizza. In Sparking Zero's case, I paid expecting for the developers to have already made the content for me to play...what I got was an, arguably, unfinished product that the developers are expecting paying customers to "complete."  Mission 100 mode was added January 2026 and is basically a mode that used to be in the PS2 entries (out of the box mind you, not 1 year later) and apparently that has a known bug on Mission 78 that makes the player auto lose for...reasons?

3.) Shallow Combat
Obviously most people are interested in a DBZ game for the combat and I will say around 80% of Sparking Zero's combat is fine. If you played the previous PS2/3 era games Sparking Zero plays similar to that...yet is not as polished. The combat itself has some odd issues. (basic rush attacks will attack "forward" past grounded enemies leaving your side/back exposed, basic rush attacks vs giant character will, somehow, start at chest level then for whatever reason begin to whiff the giant's head, regardless of difficult CPU ranges from "mindlessly roaming stage" to "plays near perfect like MKII arcade Shao Khan", etc.) Since Sparking Zero has a "Ranked mode" this game was intended to have some sort of "competitive" nature. The problem is, however, the combat is too simplistic and/or shallow in nature that 99% of the time the winning strategy is simply to get behind your opponent (as you are defenseless when an opponent is behind you) and do a really long combo...or spam blast attacks. That's basically it. In the PS2 era when these where basically single player games it was fine but if you are going to have a "competitive" game with a "rank mode" it behooves you to tweak the combat to have a "easy to pick up and play yet hard to master" game to keep players interested and not drop the game after a short time. A potential solution would have been Sparking Zero having "vanish" to be tied to resource manage via costing 2 ki bars (max bars is 5 so 2 "vanishes") so it could be a defensive way to get out of back attacks or bad spots just like in DBZ:B3 where you could teleport for 3 ki bars (max bars was 7 so 2 "teleports") That way there is a "high risk, high reward"  for using ultimate/blast attacks in competitive play (enabling mind games) along with a way to punish low skill spammers. Also in the older PS2 games, there were advanced tech like "cancels" where you could feint you were doing a smash attack, cancel, then perform a different attack to mix up enemies. The CPU at higher difficulties would feint a smash attack, only to cancel and perform an "unblockable" throw attack (which required pressing the block button at a specific time to counter the throw) then perform a blast 1/2 or ultimate if the throw connected. Feats like I just described should be the bar that separates a "skilled competitive player" in ranked matches vs an "unskilled casual player" who only plays the CPU offline. In contrast the "Peak" of Sparking Zero is you vanish, opponent counter vanish, you vanish, opponent counter vanish, etc. until someone messes up then big damage. 

4.)"Character customization" is a joke. 
On the customization screen you will see options like "outfits" and "accessories" and think "oh? Nice. I can unlock new costumes/accessories to customize characters." WRONG! Yes despite previous entries such as DBZ:BT2 (a PS2 game from 2006) offering, at least, 1 "alternate costume" via a simple color swap per character and DBZ:BT3 (a PS2 game from 2007) offered character ki aura color customization for all characters...nothing like that exists in Sparking Zero. For the main characters Goku, Gohan, Vegeta, Trunks, etc. you can change their costume to various looks they had throughout the series. The remaining roster of character's "outfit" option is a single "default 1" (Not even "recolors") and for "accessories" if the character had it in the show then you can equip it. For example if a saiyan had a scouter you can choose to equip it or not under "accessories." Unfortuately, that means approximately 85% of the cast, cannot even equip an accessory (not even a basic "halo")

From a fellow PS2-era BT3 player, this game is a dynamic yet nostalgic reboot of the series with so many great pros that far diminish the (valid) cons. Absolutely recommend it to BOTH Dragonball and non-Dragonball fans as just a good combat game.

Looking at its face value core gameplay- this arena fighter's hand-to-hand combos and Ki ability based combat is jawdropping. The hand-to-hand combat feels so tight and intuitive once YOU LEARN IT. It gets quite deep but if you practice enough, it becomes muscle memory. You can chain combo opponents into oblivion but theres also a variety of defensive counters to help you against getting combo'd (Not to mention the offensive counters to the defensive counters x_x) which is best left to the surprisingly in-depth tutorial system to explain. Just trust that you will feel extremely rewarded to learn how to extend you chain combos. Whether in singleplayer or multiplayer- you can get by with typical button mashing- but the challenge will ramp up eventually in both areas where you WILL need to learn the combat mechanics.

With the Ki based abilities (beams, blasts, bombs etc)- what can I say- it feels as stunning as it did back in the good old BT3 days, except it now also LOOKS stunning in Unreal Engine. The colours, particle effects, fidelity and all just FEEL right.
 
Coming to my cons for this game- like everyone who's reviewed the game so far has echoed- the story mode (episode battle) feels incredibly lack-lustre and I cant believe this series which used to be renowned with excellent singleplayer modes has resorted to Sparking Zero's approach of powerpoint-esque slides with barren dialogue style of storytelling. It takes away SO MUCH of the emotion that you may have gotten from watching the anime or reading the mangas, especially since the game RUSHES through the arcs so fast you would miss them if you blinked. Now the speed of storytelling may be a good or bad thing depending on what type of player you are. So if you ARE looking for a serious, cinematic story based Dragonball game- stick to Kakarot. You would think after 13 years since the last entry, they would have put more effort into the main gamemode for many players.
HOWEVER, one factor absolutely SAVES the episode battles- the What-IF scenarios (sparking episodes). There's quite a respectable amount of them in the game. Some of them may end very abruptly with little open ended interpretation, some may go through unexplored paths in certain arcs that will eventually line back up with the main canon timeline, BUT some of them create entirely new timeline arcs that are vastly different from canon. And its the combination of ALL of these sparking episodes that makes the episode battles worth playing, as each sparking episode has different unlock criterias. 

Next, the lack of any OTHER gamemodes other than the various tournament gamemodes, most of them feeling just the same as each other with minor rule changes.

Further, A lot of the playable characters are straight up locked behind long gameplay commitment. As your player level rises by playing, you unlock the ability to purchase more characters in the shop. Alternatively, a vast range of characters are also unlocked by completing episode battles AND sparking episodes. So, you gotta commit quite a while to unlock everything. I personally dont mind this as its Bandai's way of ensuring some sort of gameplay loop and replayability. But unlocking all characters personally took me around 25 hours of gameplay. 

Finally, the multiplayer- be aware that this game IS unbalanced with its character rosters, The obviously stronger characters perform and intuitively feel better than the obviously weaker characters. This is part of the Tenkaichi/Sparking series identity to make you FEEL powerful when playing as those characters. You WILL feel proud if you take down stronger characters with weaker characters if you are better than your opponent player if thats your thing. But if you expect all characters to be equal- this is not it. PS.- I DONT MIND THIS, I ENJOY THIS ASPECT OF UNBALANCEDNESS.

TL;DR Incredibly strong fighting game, let alone a dragonball game with high highs but mediocre lows. Graphics are excellent. combat is butter, what-if stories are crazy, strong characters FEEL powerful, multiplayer can be fun if accepting the series identiy.

[h1]Preface[/h1]
What a time to be alive. Despite the flaws Sparking Zero may have, whoever grew up like I did with the Budokai/Tenkaichi series will be inclined to agree what an enormous comeback this is for Dragon Ball. Many reviews have already paid tribute to the passing of Toriyama, and I can only add to that fact by saying Dragon Ball will never die in our hearts.

[h1]Positives[/h1]
[b]Combat[/b]
The bread and butter appeal of any DRAGON BALL game that belongs to the FIGHTING GAME genre; and the combat is at its PEAK with Sparking Zero. With only 4 hours of playtime so far, I've been immersed in just exploring different combo routes and making my flow charts as smooth and cool as possible. Combo extensions and variety of cancels? Check. Different types of blasts that are useful in a plethora of situations? Check. Four to five ways to counter enemy flow? Check. [insert ecstasy meme here]

[b]Sub Chapters[/b]
Without any major spoilers, I just want to add that I was pleasantly impressed with some of the fan service here. It's obvious they made the "main story" paths fairly linear and simple, and the cutscenes are somewhat lazy. But they put some effort into making the sub chapters (aka alternate what-if scenarios) pretty intriguing. One example is the route in Goku's story where they beat the Frieza army early on when they arrive on Earth and Vegeta achieves Super Saiyan following Goku's ascension when they meet on Namek. Super Saiyan Vegeta in original Saiyan armor in a vg cutscene w/ voice acting? Thank you 2024.

[b]Online[/b]
Haven't touched this yet, but have heard good things about it so far. I'd like to think/hope they didn't mess this part up in a Dragon Ball game that everyone's been waiting for.

[h1]Negatives[/h1]
[b]Bandai Namco-esque Quality[/b]
The title of this category may be questionable, but something about Bandai Namco-published games have bothered me for the past decade. Obviously, this doesn't trump my satisfaction that this game even exists, but other than the combat, their games seem to drop the ball in other aspects by not living up their potential. I'm talking specifically about factors like customization, offline replayability, and just overall "depth" to the game quality.

All in all, character customization seems lackluster at best; was hoping for different color palettes for characters this time around but why do they always think good customization = just tacking on different trash items on characters (I'm looking at you UNS)? Capsule items is such a lazy and unnecessary mechanic that more or less breaks immersion in fights, lack of super/blast customization is underwhelming considering we've had the feature in past games, story episodes feel lazy and it's obvious, and the character select screen/roster is messy to say the least. They should have hired someone to sit down and say "OK, we have different characters with different transformations, how can we make the roster as neat as possible without having 17 different variations of the same character take up half the screen?"

[h1]Conclusion[/h1]
[b]Final Verdict: A-[/b]
With all said and done, I'd like to add that I am one of the OG purists (like with many other beloved franchises - of all cultures - that have been gutted in the past decade) who dislike Dragon Ball SUPER with a passion. The path this series could have taken after mainline Z and even the controversial GT could have been exponentially better than what Super came up with, but some of us had to bite our tongues and settle for less. Regardless, the game itself is a solid A-tier game in its own right (mainly due to gameplay), both as a DB game and a fighting game with easy-to-pick up and hard-to-master mechanics.

PS: Don't buy the DLC if you hate Super, just stick with the base roster and you'll have just as good a time since the main appeal of these games aren't exactly the DLC "stories" (if not better). Cabba? Kefla? They don't exist in my book. The Super Saiyan "tingly back feeling" still has me LOLing to this very day. That's like back in high school when we pretended to go Super Saiyan on the toilet.

It's a game made for fun, which I respect. I recommend staying away from ranked, mainly because you'll be fighting the same characters over and over. I've enjoyed the offline modes as well as casually playing 1v1 online. It's fun to duke it out with other players as lesser known/played/powerful dragon ball characters. Why Sparking Zero is good:
1) up to date roster
2) up to date graphics
3) combat mimics the anime perfectly (this cannot be overstated)
If this is all you care about, then I recommend it.

Why Sparking Zero is still trash overall (From someone who expected better):
1) It is missing content like extra game modes that were present in every other dragonball game dating back 20 years. Bonus Battle mode and scenario builder are good but older games had much more. there's no excuse for a game thats had this long to develop to be released with less content than games that would be considered ancient by today.

2) similar to the above, it's missing characters. while it does have newer up to date characters from Super, it's still missing the characters from the previous game BT3. Specifically it's missing all the Dragonball characters and GT characters Nuova and Eis which I expect to be released later.

3) The game costs $110 if you want the full game. And yes, in this case, this is literally what's happening. The game was released with characters already created (Beast Gohan and Orange Piccolo) yet they were specifically held back, despite being finished. So this isn't "extra bonus content" this is "we already have this done but if you want it you gotta pay the real price". And if you think there will only be 1 pass, you're a fool. The true full price for this title will be $200 before its sunset. You can argue thats a symptom of modern gaming, but if you're going to say this is BT4 then i'm going to count this as a strike against it for the purpose of being a true sequel rather than a cash grab.

4) Game was released in a poor state (this will be a collection of minor problems)
a) Damage Balancing: While I have no problem with 'balance' as far as the characters are concerned, I do have a problem with the sheer amount of damage the characters all deal as it relates to the health bars they have available. 1 single combo from Sparking into an Ult can deal 5 bars of health easily and i'm sure you could do more against someone that doesn't break the combo. You start with 3. this shouldn't be possible. Ults shouldn't do 3 bars of damage. I shouldn't be able to combo into 5 bars of damage. This isn't a "SS4 Gogeta is OP" so much as "all characters need to have nerfed damage so that these fights can feel anime accurate, a fight shouldn't be over as soon as someone lands sparking mode 30 seconds into a match"

b) Lack of clarity: Missions are not clear what the objective is. You do not know how many enemies you are fighting until you clear the mission, so you don't know to what extent you have to "try" until you've beaten it. Missions should clearly indicate how many enemies you're up against so you know if its a "go into sparking and start spamming because this is a 1v5 fight and there's no other reasonable way to win this situation" or a "oh its 1v1 so I can do melee only with no ki at all and just have fun". Additionally, they do not indicate what the requirements are for the bonus missions. "Beat the enemy fast" is what almost all of them say, but how fast? And there's not always a voice cue to indicate when you took too long. Additionally, this is bad game design because it forces you to use the OP sparking->Ult combo to shred the enemy as fast as possible, there's no other way to clear these bonus objectives. Also, people have made so many threads about beating Jiren or Goku and not completing the story because the game just isn't clear that there's two paths and you did the wrong one. Game should be more clear.

c) Incomplete details:  Virtually no character interactions. Every character interaction can be seen in Zeno's menu, and its something like 60 or so. Thats pathetic. There's no reason you couldn't have people read a few more lines each, you wanted this game to be an anime accurate, anime immersive, but yet you couldn't find the budget to make characters have dialogue. Bardock has lines though, so thats good. But Gohan really got snubbed. I had something else for this but forgot while I was writing.

d) No sense of accomplishment: from unlocking all the items by spending Zeni you got from the dragonballs or winning a fight because you ult'd in the first 30 seconds, theres no real sense of accomplishment in this game as its all so trivial. I have to handicap myself so that I feel like I actually did something. I can't even use super attacks because it feels like its cheating, as it trivializes the entire experience when the fight is half over the moment you stop pushing square and decide to push L2 for a change. Even the missions that are difficult do not leave me feeling accomplished because I only beat them by using the only tactic thats viable in a 1v4 or 1v5 which is to rely on sparking mode, as you cannot possibly win these fights otherwise, and i say that as a melee main. 

e) Bulma


tl;dr I think its a fun game, nice to look at, if you don't care too much then its great, I recommend it. But I expected better and personally view this as a soulless cash grab, I genuinely feel insulted, this is from someone whose played every dragonball game since Ultimate Battle 22.

If you're someone who wants a balanced online fighting game with an active playerbase, look elsewhere.

The game isn't perfect. It's got some weird holes in the roster and the combat falls apart if you approach it competitively. The scummy AI in the later story / higher difficulties pretty much pigeonholes you into a boring playstyle. I don't think anyone really wanted 2+ Daima DLCs spread out over a year, but they were probably forced by Toei / Bamco to do that. Hopefully we get follow up DLC with more ideal missing characters like Super 17 and SSJ Caulifla.

Nonetheless I *strongly* disagree with the rest of the criticism of the game. If you're someone like me who grew up with the Budokai Tenkaichi games and dreamed of what a modern sequel could be, then you've come to the right place. The roster it *does* have is fantastic. The graphics are gorgeous. The single player story is *massive* compared to BT1 and BT3 (BT2 is still the most robust story mode). The create-a-battle thing is surprisingly robust. The giant checklist of stuff to do from Whis and Lord Xeno are sort of busy work, but they also encourage you to try out the whole roster and see unique interactions instead of just playing SSB Gogeta vs LSSJ Broly for the 1,000th time. The entire roster can be unlocked by playing in any way, meaning that you never have to touch the story mode if you don't want to. The offline free battle modes are admittedly a bit lacking. It would have been nice to have a tower and/or survival mode like we had in BT3. But god forbid people remember what it's like to make your own fun in a game. I've spent dozens of hours just fighting the CPU in free battle to try out different teams, matchups and interactions. If I get no more characters after DLC 3 then I'll *still* play this game for years to come, just like I have with BT3. And that's before considering what the modding community will come up with over the years.

I waded through Ultimate Tenkaichi, Battle of Z, an incomplete Budokai remaster that's *still* trapped on PS3, and *17 years of replaying BT3* while hoping for a game like this.

This idea that a game is "dead" when active development on it slows down after release is getting really old. This isn't a live service game. It *shouldn't be* a live service game. imo the only reason it *has* online is because fans would bitch and moan if it didn't. But it's built upon a foundation that cares much more about delivering a fun Dragon Ball experience to play alone or with friends than it does about ranked ladders.

Yes, Xenoverse 2 is more content rich in a lot of ways, but it's also got aspects that range from tedious to infuriating between its awful minigames and AI that has been proven to literally cheat. And it's more of an Action RPG / fighter hybrid, whereas this is an Arena fighter. I'm glad that both exist, and we even have FighterZ for that classic 2d fighting feel. It's a good time to be a Dragon Ball fan.

tl;dr: This is a Dragon Ball fanservice sandbox, as it should be, not an online competitive fighting game. If that's what you want then you'll have a great time and I 100% recommend it. If it isn't, you've got better options.

Very fun but flawed game that is not worth the price imo. The actual game play (when its not being buggy) is extremely fun and is exactly what I wanted from a Tenkaichi sequel. The issue comes from everything else the game has to offer. The story mode is awful. Literal power point slides without voice acting in a $70 (or $100 if you bought the other versions) is silly. The "what ifs" consists of "beat X in 10 seconds all while they vanish every breath you take and pummel you with ki blasts before you can spam the sparking mode". You can't turn down the difficulty if you want to access the alternate paths either so you're stuck fumbling with the cheesy AI. The what ifs themselves are bad outside of a few. Most of them literally ends with your character defeating the bad guy early and rolling credits lol. Vegetas story ends after the Kid Buu fight despite the fact that he did indeed play a massive role in Super. Where are the "Vegeta turns into a Saiyan God against Beerus", "Vegeta defeats Golden Frieza", "Vegeta defeats Goku Black" what ifs? Why can't we do Vegeta vs Toppo despite the fact that the TOP stage, Blue Evo, and GOD Toppo are all in the game and ready to use at any time? Why start with DBS Trunks rather than give us Z Trunks? So many cool what ifs are just missing right there. "What if Gohan survived against the Androids", "What if Trunks went too far back in time", "What if Trunks came back during the Buu arc", etc. Very disappointing. The online is a joke as well. I don't mind people using Gogeta, Jiren or MUI but I absolutely hate it when my controls just up and crap out on me every few matches. Can't transform, swap characters, or do specials for some godly reason. Stages are also bad in this game. Where is glacier, Mount Paizou, Hell, or Space? Why do I get stuck in the terrain so often? Finally, the customization options might as well not be there cause outside of Goku and Vegeta you can't customize anything lol. Can't customize a characters move set either despite that being advertized ala Raging Blast. I've been playing these games since BT1 came out all the way back in 2005 so it does sting to be so disappointed in Sparking Zero seeing how much the previous titles meant to me growing up, but this game simply is not worth the price tag. Wait for sale, and for them to patch out the bugs before buying imo.
